events.credibility_reason: The 2020 text was never read. Nothing in the record shows it contains an embedded realisation rather than only the combinatorial map, and the 2026 paper calls itself a coordinate realisation of that earlier work.

8 of the 28 face pairs share two edges. If 'polyhedron' is read strictly, so that two faces meet in at most one edge, the example does not qualify. Embeddedness rests only on the author's own exact checks.
Same convention issue: 8 face pairs share two collinear edges. The only verification is the authors' own exact rational checks plus an unnamed AI framework.
events.ai_basis: The authors acknowledge the significant use of artificial intelligence (Claude) in most phases of this work.

why: The statement asks only whether such a polyhedron exists, so one embedded, non-convex, eight-face example in which every pair of faces shares an edge answers it in full. Both 2026 preprints give such an example, explicitly, with exact integer or rational coordinates, and anyone can check them by computer algebra. That makes each of them whole, checkable and a witness. I marked both doubtful rather than credible for two reasons. First, the record leaves open whether two faces may share two edges, and MathWorld points out the stricter polyhedral-complex convention. Second, neither example has been checked by anyone other than its authors. The literal wording, 'share an edge', is met by pairs sharing at least one edge, so I answered on that reading. AI role: Mizhaev's 'assistance with certain calculations' does not say ChatGPT produced any of the construction, so it is none. Röst and Vígh credit Claude with 'significant use … in most phases' of a work whose result is a construction found by search, and I read that as Claude supplying part of the mathematics, so assisted. This was a close call against none, because the quote never says which part Claude produced. The 2020 OSF preprint is unread, so I gave it no scope and cannot place the construction before the snapshot. The 2008, 2016, 2002 and 2025 events are about vertex triangulations, immersions, the seven-face case, or a failed search, so none of them is the question.
doubts: (1) Whether doubled-edge face pairs are acceptable under the intended meaning of 'polyhedron' and 'share an edge'. Under the strict reading, neither 2026 example qualifies. (2) The 2020 OSF preprint is unread. If it already gives an embedded realisation, the problem moved before the snapshot. (3) The Röst–Vígh 'assisted' call rests on a broad acknowledgement and does not show what Claude produced. (4) No independent third party has rerun the coordinate checks for either example.
